stimulus.body: The handover prints 'ALLERGY: penicillin' in capitals and bold, then lists routine care in normal text.

questions.stem: Why is the allergy printed in capitals and bold?

options.text: To make the allergy stand out for safety.
To shout at the next shift.
To show the allergy is not serious.
To save space in the record.

questions.explanation: Capitalised bold text makes a safety-critical allergy stand out. The other options misread emphasis.
questions.hint: Why emphasise a safety fact?

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify a euphemism about confusion
questions.stem: A handover says a patient is 'a bit muddled' today; what does this most likely soften?

options.text: It softens possible confusion or disorientation.
It means the patient is physically tangled in sheets.
It means the patient is angry and loud.
It means the patient is very intelligent.
options.misconception: reverses the meaning of the phrase

questions.explanation: 'A bit muddled' softens confusion or disorientation. The literal, anger and reversed readings are wrong.
questions.hint: Think of mental clarity, not sheets or anger.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Figurative meaning of a fixed expression
questions.learningObjective: interpret a fixed expression about decline
questions.stem: Nurse Lee writes that a patient 'went downhill' overnight; what does this signal?

options.text: The patient's condition worsened.
The patient walked down a hill outside.
The patient improved rapidly.
options.misconception: reverses the meaning of the expression

options.text: The patient is being discharged downhill.

questions.explanation: Going downhill signals worsening. The literal, reversed and invented readings are wrong.
questions.hint: Think of decline, not a real hill.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain the purpose of a mixed-register notice
questions.stem: Why might a notice use a formal rule but a casual opening?

answer.exemplar: The casual opening builds rapport and welcomes readers, while the formal rule still states the obligation clearly, so warmth and authority coexist.

questions.explanation: Warmth and authority can coexist in one notice. Neither part cancels the other.
questions.hint: Separate welcome from obligation.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a conclusion follows from evidence

stimulus.body: The handover notes that the patient drank water twice and passed urine once during the shift. No other fluids were recorded.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The patient is fully hydrated and needs no monitoring.
The patient took water twice and urinated once this shift.
The patient is dehydrated and at risk.
Fluid balance is normal for all patients.

questions.explanation: The evidence supports only the observed counts this shift. Hydration status, dehydration and universal norms all overreach.
questions.hint: Stick to the recorded counts.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: spot an informal marker in a notice
questions.stem: Which phrase most clearly marks an informal register?

options.text: 'observations recorded per protocol'
'patient settled and comfortable'
'we had a good yarn with the patient'
'fluid balance chart completed'
options.misconception: mistakes a record entry for informal

questions.explanation: 'Good yarn' is casual and marks informality. The other options are clinical or record language.
questions.hint: Look for casual, conversational wording.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: infer purpose from a handover that uses a table
questions.stem: A handover presents observations in a table with times; what is the likely purpose of that shape?

options.text: To let readers track changes over time at a glance.
To hide abnormal values among many numbers.
To make the record longer and more impressive.
To replace the need for any narrative at all.

questions.explanation: A time-based table helps readers see trends quickly. The other options misread its function.
questions.hint: Why use times in columns?

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify a euphemism about breathing
questions.stem: Why might a nurse write 'a bit breathless' instead of 'struggling to breathe'?

answer.exemplar: 'A bit breathless' softens distress and keeps the record calm, but it can hide severity and delay escalation of care.

questions.explanation: The softer phrase protects tone but can hide severity. Escalation may then be delayed.
questions.hint: Name the softened fact and the risk.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Figurative meaning of a fixed expression
questions.learningObjective: interpret a fixed expression about effort

stimulus.body: The note says the patient 'pushed through' the physiotherapy session despite fatigue.

questions.stem: What does 'pushed through' most likely mean?

options.text: The patient completed the session despite difficulty.
The patient physically pushed equipment through a door.
The patient refused to attend physiotherapy.
options.misconception: reverses the meaning of the expression

options.text: The patient found the session easy and quick.

questions.explanation: Pushing through means completing despite difficulty. The literal, reversed and easy readings are wrong.
questions.hint: Think of effort despite fatigue.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: classify a notice's register from its wording
questions.stem: A notice reads 'Staff must attend the briefing' and ends 'see you there'; what is the overall register?

options.text: Fully informal, because of the closing.
options.misconception: lets the closer override the rule

options.text: Formal rule with a friendly closer.
Fully formal, with no warmth at all.
Neither formal nor informal, just neutral.
options.misconception: misses both the duty and the warmth

questions.explanation: The rule is formal and the closer is friendly, so the notice mixes registers. The fully-formal and fully-informal readings miss one half.
questions.hint: Consider both parts together.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify an overclaim about mobility
questions.stem: A handover says 'walked to the bathroom' after one assisted trip; what can be claimed?

options.text: The patient can walk to the bathroom alone always.
The patient walked to the bathroom with assistance this time.
The patient is now fully mobile and independent.
The trip proves the patient needs no help ever.

questions.explanation: One assisted trip supports only that instance. Independence and always overreach.
questions.hint: Keep the claim to the assisted trip.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain why formality matters in a handover
questions.stem: Why does formality in a handover protect patients?

answer.exemplar: Formal wording reduces ambiguity and creates an accountable record, so the next shift can act on clear facts rather than guess at casual hints.

questions.explanation: Formality reduces ambiguity and supports accountability. Casual wording risks unclear action.
questions.hint: Think about clarity and accountability.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: infer purpose from a handover that uses a heading

stimulus.body: The handover uses the heading 'RISK' before a single line about falls, then 'ROUTINE' before the rest.

questions.stem: What does the 'RISK' heading most likely do?

options.text: Mark the risk as a distinct, priority section.
Hide the risk from busy readers.
Prove the risk is minor and forgettable.
Replace the need to read the line itself.

questions.explanation: A 'RISK' heading flags a priority section. The other options misread its function.
questions.hint: Why label a section 'RISK'?

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify a euphemism about sleep
questions.stem: A handover says a patient 'dozed on and off' overnight; what does this most likely soften?

options.text: It softens fragmented, poor-quality sleep.
It means the patient was fully asleep all night.
It means the patient was awake and working.
It means the patient refused to sleep at all.

questions.explanation: 'Dozed on and off' softens fragmented sleep. The fully-asleep, working and refused readings are wrong.
questions.hint: Think of interrupted sleep.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Figurative meaning of a fixed expression
questions.learningObjective: paraphrase a fixed expression for safety
questions.stem: Nurse Kim writes that a patient 'is out of the woods' after surgery; what does this imply?

options.text: The patient has passed the most dangerous period.
The patient is literally in a forest now.
The patient needs no further monitoring.
The patient's condition has worsened.
options.misconception: reverses the meaning of the expression

questions.explanation: Being out of the woods signals passing the worst danger, not full recovery. The literal, overreach and reversed readings are wrong.
questions.hint: Think of danger passed, not care ended.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain why a notice mixes registers
questions.stem: Why might a notice mix a formal deadline with a casual greeting?

answer.exemplar: The formal deadline makes the obligation clear and accountable, while the casual greeting keeps the message approachable and human.

questions.explanation: Obligation and approachability can coexist. Neither cancels the other.
questions.hint: Separate duty from tone.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: judge a claim's support from one observation

stimulus.body: The handover records that the patient ate a full breakfast and felt well afterward. No other meals were observed.

questions.stem: What is the safest claim?

options.text: The patient's nutrition is now fully adequate.
The patient ate a full breakfast and felt well after it.
The patient will eat well at every future meal.
The patient was hungry before breakfast.
options.misconception: invents a prior state not recorded

questions.explanation: One meal supports only that instance. Nutrition adequacy and future eating overreach; prior hunger is unrecorded.
questions.hint: Stay with the observed breakfast.
